ideas.title: OpenAI Shipped an Overnight Employee and Called It a Coding Tool
ideas.trend: OpenAI's Codex launched 'Locked Use' last week, allowing its agent to operate macOS apps behind a locked screen; 4M weekly users already active, feature blocked in EU/UK/Switzerland at launch
ideas.consensus: Codex is an increasingly capable coding and automation assistant with useful new workflow features
ideas.angle: The 'Codex' brand is the distraction. This is the first mass-deployed autonomous agent with persistent OS-level permissions operating production systems outside active user sessions, and enterprise security has no policy framework for it yet

content_pack.x_longform:
OpenAI just shipped an autonomous computer operator and named it after a 2021 code generator.

Codex's Locked Use, announced last week, lets the agent operate macOS applications behind a locked screen. It installs an Apple authorization plugin, temporarily unlocks the device, runs tasks using its own cursor, and relocks if the user touches the keyboard. It sees the screen. It clicks. It types. The user is asleep.

The product already runs on over 4 million devices per week.

The enterprise security implication is structural. Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions at the OS level sit outside every endpoint detection and response playbook written before 2025. An EDR tool monitoring for unauthorized screen capture cannot distinguish between a threat actor and Codex executing a task its user authorized three days ago. Enterprise legal and IT teams have no policy framework for this yet. Per OpenAI's own developer documentation, enterprise administrators receive managed configuration controls they have not been briefed on.

The permission chain matters. Codex requests Accessibility access, used by screen readers and automation tools, plus Screen Recording, used by remote desktop and screen capture applications. These are macOS system-level permissions that persist across reboots. Not scoped to a session. Once granted, Codex can interact with any application the user can interact with, including banking apps, internal HR systems, legal document management platforms, and securities trading terminals. The agent's actions are logged within OpenAI's telemetry, not within enterprise data loss prevention systems unless IT explicitly builds that bridge.

Financial services compliance risk is real. FINRA requires broker-dealers to retain records of all business communications. An AI agent executing trades, drafting client notes, or updating records autonomously, outside active user sessions, fits that definition. Existing guidance does not address it.

OpenAI blocked Locked Use at launch in the European Economic Area, the UK, and Switzerland. Three of the world's most active digital consumer protection jurisdictions declined to permit OS-level AI agents before their regulatory guidance is ready. The rest of the world shipped first.

That regulatory gap is the real signal. When GDPR applied to cookies in 2018, European users saw consent prompts for two years before equivalent US policy emerged. The EU block is not a restriction. It is a six-to-twelve-month preview of the compliance work every enterprise operating globally will have to do anyway.

The historical parallels are consistent. Enterprise email arrived in the 1990s and most large firms spent five to eight years blocking it under legal hold and discovery risk before building the compliance infrastructure to manage it. SaaS adoption from 2010 to 2018 followed the same arc: shadow IT drove adoption, compliance teams played catch-up, policy was written after the usage was already embedded. API integrations from 2015 onward repeated the pattern. Scoped tokens and OAuth emerged as the compliance layer after adoption, not before.

Each time, governance was written after the capability deployed. The capability won every time.

In 2000, Napster was a music player. In 2007, the iPhone was a phone. In 2026, Codex is a coding tool.

The name is the distraction. The permission model is the product.
content_pack.x_thread:
1/ OpenAI shipped an autonomous computer operator and named it after a 2021 code generator. Codex's Locked Use operates macOS apps behind a locked screen. The user is asleep. The agent is working.

2/ How it works: installs an Apple auth plugin, temporarily unlocks the Mac, runs tasks with its own cursor, relocks if you touch the keyboard. Accessibility + Screen Recording at OS level. No API required for any app.

3/ Already on 4 million devices per week. Blocked at launch in the EU, UK, and Switzerland. Three major consumer protection jurisdictions said not before their governance guidance is ready. The rest of the world shipped first.

4/ Enterprise IT has no playbook for this. EDR tools monitoring for unauthorized screen capture cannot distinguish a threat actor from Codex running a scheduled task. AI agents with OS-level permissions sit outside every endpoint security framework written before 2025.

5/ Financial services compliance gap is real. FINRA requires retention of all business communications. An AI agent executing trades, drafting client notes, or updating records outside user sessions fits that definition. Guidance does not exist yet.

6/ The pattern: enterprise email blocked 5-8 years under legal hold risk, compliance infrastructure built around it. SaaS shadow IT drove adoption, policy caught up. APIs the same. OS-level agents are the next cycle.

7/ OpenAI did not ship a coding tool. The 2021 Codex brand is still on the box. The 2026 product operates your email client, file system, calendar, and browser while you sleep.

8/ In 2000, Napster was a music player. In 2007, the iPhone was a phone. In 2026, Codex is a coding tool. The name is the distraction. The permission model is the product.
content_pack.substack_draft:
The conventional read on Codex is that OpenAI is steadily improving its developer tooling. Better code completion, smarter review, now better automation. A capable product getting incrementally more useful.

The actual product that shipped last week operates macOS applications behind a locked screen, using its own cursor, reading your screen, clicking through interfaces, with Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions that persist across reboots. It runs on 4 million devices per week. It is blocked at launch in the EU and UK, before their own regulatory guidance is written.

That is not incremental developer tooling. That is an autonomous agent with persistent OS-level access to production systems, deploying into enterprises that have no endpoint security policy for it yet.

I find myself genuinely unsure whether the governance will catch up fast enough this time. Enterprise email, SaaS tools, and API integrations all followed the same arc: the technology deployed before the compliance infrastructure existed, and the compliance infrastructure was eventually written around the technology rather than before it. Whether that arc serves organizations well in this case is an open question. AI agents with OS-level permissions in financial services or healthcare are a different risk profile than agents helping developers autocomplete functions. I am not sure the historical arc guarantees a good outcome here, only a familiar one.

ideas.title: A $29M Startup Just Put a Price Tag on the Transformer's Biggest Flaw
ideas.trend: SubQ from Subquadratic launched May 5 as the first claimed subquadratic LLM, raising $29M seed; VentureBeat ran skepticism piece; researchers demand independent benchmark verification
ideas.consensus: SubQ is either a major architectural breakthrough or unverified hype, awaiting independent benchmarks
ideas.angle: Both framings miss the operational signal: $29M of institutional capital moved not because SubQ is proven but because the transformer's quadratic scaling is a real constraint every major lab is paying nine figures to work around

content_pack.x_longform:
Every major AI lab is spending nine figures this year working around the transformer's attention scaling. A 12-person Miami startup raised $29 million this month claiming to have solved it.

SubQ, from Subquadratic, shipped as the first LLM built on a fully subquadratic architecture. Compute scales linearly with context length rather than quadratically. At 12-million-token contexts, the team reports 1,000x compute reduction versus comparable frontier models. VentureBeat ran the binary headline: "AI Theranos or the biggest breakthrough since the transformer." Researchers flagged that the benchmarks have not been independently reproduced. The community split on the same evidence.

Both framings miss the operational signal. The transformer's quadratic scaling is not a hypothetical concern. It is why GPU clusters cost $100 billion to build. It is the single largest cost lever in frontier AI infrastructure. Every hyperscaler's 2026 capex plan is partly a workaround for an architectural constraint baked in since 2017.

The $29 million seed round signals that institutional capital assessed the problem, decided it was real enough, and bet on the team claiming to fix it. Whether SubQ delivers is a separate question from whether the problem is worth $29 million to point at correctly.

Capital flows to constraints before it flows to solutions. This constraint is quadratic.
content_pack.x_thread:
1/ Every major AI lab is spending nine figures working around the transformer's attention scaling. A 12-person Miami startup raised $29M this month claiming to have solved it.

2/ SubQ from Subquadratic: first LLM on a fully subquadratic architecture. Compute scales linearly with context length, not quadratically. Claims 1,000x compute reduction at 12M tokens vs comparable frontier models. Architecture: SSA (Subquadratic Selective Attention).

3/ VentureBeat: "AI Theranos or the biggest breakthrough since the transformer." Researchers flagged benchmarks not independently reproduced. The community split on the same evidence.

4/ Both framings miss the operational point. The transformer's quadratic scaling is why GPU clusters cost $100 billion to build. It is the single largest cost lever in frontier AI infrastructure. Every major capex plan this year is partly a workaround for architecture baked in since 2017.

5/ What the $29M seed round actually means: institutional capital assessed the constraint, decided it was real, and bet on the team claiming to fix it. Whether SubQ delivers is a separate question from whether the constraint is worth betting against.

6/ Capital flows to constraints before it flows to solutions. This constraint is quadratic.
content_pack.substack_draft:
$29 million. That number is doing a lot of work in the SubQ story.

SubQ, from a Miami startup called Subquadratic, launched this month as what it claims is the first LLM built on a fully subquadratic architecture. The claim: its attention mechanism scales linearly with context length rather than quadratically. At 12-million-token contexts, the team says compute drops 1,000x versus comparable frontier models. Researchers are skeptical. The benchmarks have not been independently reproduced. VentureBeat ran a headline calling it either the biggest AI breakthrough since the transformer or the next Theranos.

What I keep returning to is not whether the model works but why the money moved. The transformer's quadratic scaling is not a theoretical concern. Every major lab building at the frontier runs into it. The $29 million seed round went to a team that correctly named the problem and provided enough internal evidence to move institutional investors. Whether SubQ delivers the breakthrough is a separate question from whether it identified the right constraint to attack.

I am genuinely uncertain whether non-transformer architectures can deliver frontier-quality performance at scale. The transformer won in 2017 partly because its parallelism mapped well onto GPU hardware. A subquadratic architecture needs that same hardware compatibility story, and independent benchmarks will either support or undermine the claim. Worth watching closely.

ideas.title: Brex Sold for $5 Billion. Distribution Just Named Its Price for Technology.
ideas.trend: Capital One / Brex deal expected to close mid-2026 at $5.15B, representing a 58% discount from Brex's $12.3B 2021 peak valuation
ideas.consensus: The deal reflects valuation normalization across the 2021 fintech vintage and is a win for Capital One's corporate card business
ideas.angle: Distribution pricing technology is the structural pattern of every major fintech exit. Brex built the best product. Capital One owned the network. In financial services, the network sets the exit price.

content_pack.x_longform:
$12.3 billion in 2021.

Capital One is buying Brex for $5.15 billion, a 58% haircut from peak, per Crunchbase reporting. The deal closes this summer.

The narrative heading into this acquisition is correct: Brex built the best corporate expense product in the industry. Corporate card, expense automation, real-time payments, treasury management, bill pay. A complete stack for modern finance teams, serving over 20,000 businesses including significant enterprise accounts. The product was not the constraint.

Distribution was the constraint.

Corporate financial products live inside existing banking relationships. The CFO who approves Brex is the same CFO whose operating account, line of credit, treasury, and payroll infrastructure sit at a large commercial bank. Standalone fintech wins at the margin. It wins when the large bank's product is genuinely worse and the switching cost is survivable. Brex made both bets. The category got competitive, the enterprise sales cycle lengthened, and the 2021 valuation was priced on assumptions that did not survive rate normalization.

Capital One did not build a better expense product. Capital One had 25 million US consumer accounts, a commercial card business already embedded in enterprise banking relationships, and a distribution apparatus Brex could not replicate without spending more capital than its valuation supported.

The structural pattern repeats in financial services. Marcus by Goldman Sachs built excellent deposit and lending products and struggled to cross-sell without branches. Robinhood built a generation of retail investors and spent seven years without a revenue model that scaled. Chime built 22 million accounts on top of banking infrastructure it did not own. In each case, technology created value. The distribution-native player set the price.

The 2021 thesis was that software would unbundle banking and that the unbundled pieces would be more valuable than the bundle. Capital One's acquisition price is the market's verdict on that thesis.

Brex built the product. Capital One bought the customer.
content_pack.x_thread:
1/ $12.3 billion in 2021. $5.15 billion in 2026. Capital One is buying Brex at a 58% discount from peak. Distribution just set the price for fintech's best expense product.

2/ Brex built the complete corporate finance stack: corporate card, expense automation, real-time payments, treasury, bill pay. 20,000+ business customers including significant enterprise accounts. The product was strong. Per Crunchbase, the deal closes this summer.

3/ Distribution was the constraint. Corporate CFOs buy financial products inside banking relationships. Standalone fintech wins when the bank's product is worse AND switching costs are survivable. Brex ran into both limits as the category got competitive.

4/ Capital One did not build a better expense product. Capital One had 25M US consumer accounts and a commercial card business already embedded in enterprise banking relationships. Brex could not replicate that footprint without spending more than its model allowed.

5/ The pattern: Marcus by Goldman built excellent deposit products, struggled without branches. Robinhood built 25M retail investors, no scalable revenue model for 7 years. Chime built 22M accounts on rented infrastructure. Technology creates value. Distribution prices it.

6/ The 2021 thesis: software unbundles banking. The pieces are worth more than the bundle. Capital One's $5.15B acquisition price is the market's verdict on that thesis.

7/ Brex built the product. Capital One bought the customer.
content_pack.substack_draft:
The neobank cycle is roughly 15 years old now, and the Capital One/Brex acquisition is one of the cleaner readings of where it ends up.

Brex peaked at $12.3 billion in 2021. Capital One is buying it for $5.15 billion, closing this summer. The discount is real but it is also somewhat beside the point. Brex built a genuinely strong product, corporate card, expense automation, real-time payments, treasury management, the full stack for a modern finance team. The company grew to 20,000+ business customers including significant enterprise accounts. The product was not the problem.

The part that is harder to build is the part Capital One already had: commercial banking relationships embedded inside existing enterprise accounts, a card business with real distribution, and 25 million retail accounts. Brex could not match that footprint without spending more than its valuation model allowed.

I think about the broader 2018-2021 fintech vintage and the exits look similar. Marcus by Goldman built strong deposit products and struggled to cross-sell without branches. Chime built 22 million accounts on banking infrastructure it rented. In financial services, the technology creates real value, and then a distribution-native player shows up to price what that value is worth. I am not sure whether the next wave of fintech founders has fully absorbed this. The question I keep returning to: is there a product category in financial services where technology can build its own distribution, or does the distribution layer always get to set the final price?
